%% The abstract is a short summary of the work to be presented in the
%% article.
\begin{abstract}
  Generative recommendation (GR) is an emerging paradigm where user actions are tokenized into discrete token patterns and autoregressively generated as predictions. Despite progress, two limitations persist: tokenization often under-captures fine-grained semantic relations among items, and the training objective is misaligned with ranking quality. To address this, we propose \textbf{SAGE} (\underline{S}emantic-\underline{A}ware tokenization with rankin\underline{G} guidanc\underline{E} for GR), which injects richer semantics into tokenization and aligns generation with item ranking. During vocabulary construction, SAGE begins with primitive interaction tokens and iteratively builds a multi-granular lexicon by merging pairs scored by a semantics-aware criterion that fuses item-level proximity with the local co-occurrence structure. This prioritizes units that frequently co-occur and are semantically proximal, yielding coherent, context-sensitive tokens that better preserve fine-grained relations across contexts. To reduce the gap between likelihood training and ranking evaluation, SAGE adopts a rank-aligned loss function coupled with an ensemble inference strategy, which directly optimizes the model for accurate top-$k$ ordering. Experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that SAGE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving relative improvements of up to 8.0\% in ranking accuracy.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Generative Recommendation (GR) has emerged as a scalable alternative to discriminative Sequential Recommendation (SR) models (e.g., SASRec\cite{kang2018self}, BERT4Rec\cite{sun2019bert4rec}) by reformulating prediction as autoregressive token generation over a compact vocabulary\cite{rajput2023recommender,hou2025actionpiece,geng2022recommendation,hou2025generating}. Despite this efficiency, current GR paradigms face two critical limitations regarding token semantic quality and objective alignment.

The first bottleneck lies in the \emph{semantic expressiveness of tokenization}. Early methods (e.g., TIGER\cite{rajput2023recommender}, SPM-SID\cite{singh2024better}) yield context-independent tokens, while subsequent collaborative approaches (CoST\cite{zhu2024cost}, LETTER\cite{wang2024learnable}) still under-capture fine-grained relations. Even the state-of-the-art ActionPiece\cite{hou2025actionpiece} relies on frequency-based merges that overlook item-level semantic proximity, resulting in statis\-tically frequent but semantically fragmented vocabularies. Consequently, constructing a tokenizer that balances global semantic coherence with local sequential context remains an open challenge.

Simultaneously, a \emph{discrepancy persists between generative training and ranking goals}. Most GR models optimize the pointwise Language Modeling Loss (LML)\cite{radford2018improving}, neglecting listwise ordering. Although recent methods like S-DPO\cite{chen2024softmax}, MSL\cite{wang2025msl}, and RPG\cite{hou2025generating} improve generation, they lack explicit alignment with ranking metrics, often producing models proficient at text generation but suboptimal for distinguishing hard negatives in top-$K$ lists.

To bridge these gaps, the \textbf{SAGE} (\underline{S}emantic-\underline{A}ware tokenization with rankin\underline{G} guidanc\underline{E}) framework is introduced to unify semantic fidelity with ranking-oriented optimization. 
Unlike frequency-driven approaches, SAGE constructs a context-sensitive lexicon by fusing item-level proximity with local co-occurrence, ensuring tokens are both frequently utilized and semantically coherent. 
Furthermore, the framework couples a \emph{rank-aligned} training objective with lightweight ensemble inference to explicitly bias the decoding process toward listwise quality. 
Empirical evaluations on three real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of this design, demonstrating that SAGE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in both ranking accuracy and generative quality.

  \centering
  \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{SAGE.pdf}
  \caption{Overview of the proposed SAGE framework.}
  \label{fig:SAGE}
  \Description{This is a framework of SAGE}
\end{figure}

\section{Methodology}
\subsection{Problem Formulation}
The problem of sequential recommendation is formulated as follows: given an item set $\mathcal{I}$ and a history sequence $\mathcal{S}=\{i_1,\ldots,i_{t-1}\}$ for user $u$, the objective is to predict the next item $i_t\in\mathcal{I}$. Each item is characterized by multiple content features (e.g., text, images). In this framework, the raw interaction sequence is transformed into a sequence of feature sets, where raw features are encoded into dense vectors via pretrained semantic encoders\cite{ni2022sentence} and subsequently \emph{tokenized} into discrete codes.

Specifically, Optimized Product Quantization (OPQ)\cite{ge2013optimized} is employed to derive, for each item $i$, an \emph{unordered} token tuple $(c_1^i,\ldots,c_m^i)$ with $c_1^i\in C^{(1)}=\{1,\ldots,M\}$, $c_2^i\in C^{(2)}=\{M+1,\ldots,2M\}$, etc., where $M$ denotes the codebook size per digit of the semantic ID. To mitigate feature collisions, a hash feature $h^i$ is appended, defining the initial token set as $\mathcal{B}_i=\{c_1^i,\ldots,c_m^i,h^i\}$. In contrast to \emph{ordered} semantic IDs (e.g., RQ-VAE\cite{rajput2023recommender}), this unordered design eliminates inter-token dependency and flexibly accommodates additional discrete or numeric attributes.

Consequently, the user's history becomes a time-ordered sequence of sets, $\mathcal{S}'=\{\mathcal{B}_1,\ldots,\mathcal{B}_{t-1}\}$. While the temporal order is preserved across distinct sets, the tokens within each set $\mathcal{B}_t$ remain unordered. The recommendation task is then cast as token sequence generation\cite{ge2013optimized}: the tokenizer linearizes $\mathcal{S}'$ into 
$X=\{c_1^1, \allowbreak c_2^1, \allowbreak \cdots, \allowbreak c_{l-1}^t, \allowbreak c_l^t\}$, 
and the GR model autoregressively generates future tokens 
$\{c_1^{t+1}, \allowbreak \cdots, \allowbreak c_l^{t+1}\}$, 
which are parsed as the next-item prediction $\hat{i}_{t+1}$.

\subsection{Semantic-Aware Action Sequence Tokenizer}

A high-quality vocabulary serves as the cornerstone of generative recommendation. Accordingly, the vocabulary $\mathcal{V}_0$ is initialized with primitive feature tokens, where each token denotes a singleton set containing a unique item feature. Formally, this initialization is defined as $\mathcal{V}_0=\{\, c=\{f\} \mid f \in \mathcal{F}_1 \cup \ldots \cup \mathcal{F}_m \,\}.$ Starting from this basis, a bottom-up process is adopted to iteratively merge tokens representing frequently occurring and semantically coherent feature combinations until the vocabulary reaches a predefined size $Q$.

\paragraph{Weighted Co-occurrence.}
To identify salient feature combinations, weighted co-occurrence statistics are computed. Two distinct types of co-occurrence are defined: (i) \emph{intra-set}, where tokens appear within the same item set; and (ii) \emph{inter-set}, where tokens appear in adjacent sets to capture sequential context. To reflect how the contribution of a pair depends on its type and the sizes of the participating sets, distinct weights are assigned:
\begin{equation}
\left \{
\begin{array}{ll}
w_{\text{intra}}(c_1,c_2)=w_{\text{intra}}(c_2,c_1)
=\frac{2}{|\mathcal{B}_i|},\quad c_1,c_2\in \mathcal{B}_i \\
w_{\text{inter}}(c_1,c_3) = \dfrac{1}{|\mathcal{B}_i| \cdot|\mathcal{B}_{i+1}|},\quad c_1 \in \mathcal{B}_i, c_3 \in \mathcal{B}_{i+1}
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
By traversing the entire corpus $\mathcal{C}=\{\mathcal{S}^{(1)},\mathcal{S}^{(2)},\ldots,\mathcal{S}^{(N)}\}$, the cumulative weight for any co-occurring pair $(c_k,c_l)$ is aggregated as:
\begin{equation}
\text{cnt}(c_k,c_l) \;=\; \sum_{\mathcal{S}\in \mathcal{C}}
\big[\, w_{\text{intra}}(c_k,c_l) \;+\; w_{\text{inter}}(c_k,c_l) \,\big]
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Weighted Semantics.}
Purely frequency-driven construction often suffers from \emph{semantic mismatch}, where high-frequency pairs are not necessarily semantically coherent. To enhance the vocabulary's capacity for modeling semantic diversity, a semantics-aware token weighting mechanism is introduced, leveraging pretrained item embeddings $\mathbf{e}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$. Semantic proximity is first quantified via the $k$ nearest neighbors of each item, followed by an aggregation of item-wise weights to the token level using a normalized harmonic mean. Formally, the semantic weight of token $t$ is formulated as:
\begin{equation}
w_{\text{sem}}(t) \;=\; \frac{|\mathcal{I}_t|}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}_t} \frac{1}{w(i)}}, 
\;\text{where } \;
w(i) = \frac{\rho(i)}{\bar{\rho}}, 
\rho(i) = \frac{1}{1 + \bar{d}_i / \sigma},
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{I}_t$ denotes the set of items containing token $t$, $\bar{d}_i = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}_k(i)} \allowbreak \|\mathbf{e}_i - \mathbf{e}_j\|_2$ represents the average Euclidean distance from item $i$ to its $k$ nearest neighbors, $\sigma$ is the global median distance, and $\bar{\rho} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\sum_{j \in \mathcal{I}} \rho(j)$ serves as a normalization factor. The use of harmonic-mean aggregation mitigates outlier effects, yielding robust semantic weights.

\paragraph{Iterative Update.}
The merging strategy follows the BPE protocol while integrating semantic weights. At each iteration, a priority score is calculated for every candidate pair. To ensure numerical stability and balance frequency with semantics, the priority is defined in the log domain:
\begin{equation}
\text{priority}(c_k,c_l)= \exp\!\Big[\log \text{cnt}(c_k,c_l) + \frac{\gamma}{2}\cdot\big(\log w_{\text{sem}}(c_k)+ \log w_{\text{sem}}(c_l)\big)\Big]
\end{equation}
where $\gamma$ controls the influence of semantic weights. The pair with the highest priority is merged to create a new token $c_{\text{new}}$, which inherits the log-semantic weights from its constituents:
$
   \log w_{\text{sem}}(c_{\text{new}}) \allowbreak \;=\;  \log w_{\text{sem}}(c_k)\;+\;\log w_{\text{sem}}(c_l) 
$
Following the efficient data structures and update routines in~[6], counts and weights are maintained dynamically, and the vocabulary is iteratively updated $\mathcal{V}_{i+1}=\mathcal{V}_i \cup \{c_{\text{new}}\}$ until the target size is reached, i.e., $|\mathcal{V}|=V_{\text{target}}$.

\subsection{Rank-Aligned Optimization Strategy}

To bridge the discrepancy between generative modeling and recommendation ranking, a \emph{two-stage collaborative optimization} mechanism is introduced, spanning both training and inference phases.

\paragraph{Training.}
Standard GR models typically optimize a cross-entropy loss, explicitly maximizing the likelihood of the correct item. However, this objective treats all errors equally, failing to distinguish \emph{hard negatives} from obvious ones. To mitigate this, \emph{temperature scaling} is applied to sharpen the predictive distribution:
\begin{equation}
\left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}} = -\frac{1}{|b|} \sum_{(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) \in \mathcal{b}} \sum_{t=1}^{L} \log P_\theta(y_t \mid \mathbf{y}_{<t}, \mathbf{x}), \\
P_\theta^{\tau}(y_t \mid \mathbf{y}_{<t}, \mathbf{x}) = \dfrac{\exp(p_{y_t}/\tau)}{\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} \exp(p_v/\tau)},
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
where $\tau \in (0, 1)$ acts as the temperature hyperparameter. Reducing $\tau$ compels the model to prioritize differentiating the target from high-confidence errors, thereby aligning the training objective with the ranking goal. Here, $b$ denotes the training batch, and $P_\theta$ represents the logits vector at step $t$.

\paragraph{Inference.}
During the inference phase, to bolster generation quality and ranking robustness, an \emph{ensemble voting} strategy is adopted via \emph{multi-path stochastic permutations}. Specifically, $K$ randomized encoding paths are generated per item by permuting its feature vector ($\mathbf{f}_i \rightarrow \pi(\mathbf{f}_i)$), which captures diverse feature views. Temperature-controlled beam search is performed along each path to obtain $b$ sequences, condensing candidates via ensemble voting:
\begin{equation}
\text{score}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} \sum_{j=1}^{b} \mathbb{1}\!\left[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \hat{\mathbf{y}}_k^{(j)}\right] \cdot \frac{1}{\log_2(j + 1)},
\end{equation}
where $j$ represents the rank within the $k$-th beam. The NDCG-like discount factor $1/\log_2(j+1)$ assigns greater weight to top-ranked candidates. Ultimately, the top-$N$ items with the highest scores are retrieved as the final recommendation list.

\paragraph{Objective.}
The ultimate optimization objective is formally defined as $\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}$. This objective underpins a cohesive framework: temperature scaling during training sharpens discriminative representation learning, while multi-path ensembling during inference ensures candidate diversity and ranking stability. By tightly integrating these complementary stages, the intrinsic gap between the generative paradigm and the recommendation task is effectively bridged.

\section{Experiments}
\subsection{Experimental Setup}
\textbf{Datasets.} The proposed framework is evaluated on three public real-world benchmarks: ``Beauty'' (\textbf{Beauty}), ``Sports and Outdoors'' (\textbf{Sports}), and ``CDs and Vinyl'' (\textbf{CDs}). For each user, historical reviews are treated as interaction events and arranged chronologically to form action sequences. Following the standard leave-last-out protocol, the final item in each sequence is reserved for testing, while the penultimate item is used for validation. Summary statistics of the processed data are reported in Table~\ref{tab:dataset-stats}. Performance is assessed via top-$k$ Recall and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG), with $k$ set to 5/10.

\textbf{Models and Implementation Details.} SAGE is benchmarked against a comprehensive suite of baselines: (1) ID-based sequential methods, including BERT4Rec\cite{sun2019bert4rec} and SASRec\cite{kang2018self}; (2) feature-enhanced methods, such as FDSA\cite{zhang2019feature}, S3-Rec\cite{zhou2020s3}, and VQ-Rec\cite{hou2023learning}; and (3) generative recommendation methods, including P5-CID\cite{hua2023index}, TIGER\cite{rajput2023recommender}, HSTU\cite{zhai2024actions}, SPM-SID\cite{singh2024better}, and ActionPiece\cite{hou2025actionpiece}. Following~\cite{hou2025actionpiece}, a T5-like encoder-decoder Transformer architecture is adopted, featuring four layers for both the encoder and decoder. The multi-head attention module consists of six heads, each with a dimension of 64. The learning rate is tuned within $\{1 \times 10^{-3}, 3 \times 10^{-3}, 5 \times10^{-3}\}$ with 10,000 warm-up steps, and weight decay is selected from $\{0.07, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2\}$. All models are trained with a batch size of 256, utilizing early stopping and five repeated runs with distinct random seeds.

\subsection{Overall Performance}
SAGE consistently outperforms all baselines across Recall@K and NDCG@K metrics. This superiority is attributed to three synergistic components: (i) a semantics-aware tokenizer that integrates item-level proximity with co-occurrence statistics, constructing a discriminative and context-sensitive vocabulary; (ii) a rank-aligned training objective that reorients generation toward listwise quality rather than sole next-token likelihood; and (iii) a lightweight ensemble inference scheme that aggregates stable, high-quality sequences under stochastic permutations. Collectively, these elements ensure coherent tokenization, sharper top-$K$ ordering, and robust decoding, driving the significant gains observed in Table~\ref{tab:amazon-comp}.

\subsection{Ablation Analysis}
Table \ref{tab:ablation} reports NDCG@10 under incremental variants. The degraded results of \textit{w/ feature} (using raw item features as tokens) versus \textit{w/ cnt} highlight the necessity of learning reusable sub-item units via frequency-driven merging. Adding semantic weighting (\textit{w/ cnt+sem}) further improves upon pure frequency, indicating that proximity-aware merges reduce spurious high-frequency combinations. Replacing CE with the rank-aligned loss (\textit{w/ rank}) yields additional gains, suggesting better alignment with listwise evaluation. Enabling ensemble inference (\textit{w/ ensemble}) brings consistent robustness improvements by aggregating stable hypotheses across stochastic paths. The full model SAGE attains the best performance on all three datasets, with the largest relative gains on Sports/CDs, implying stronger benefits under sparser interactions and larger catalogs.

\section{Conclusion}

We present SAGE, an effective generative recommendation framework that unifies semantics-aware tokenization, a rank-aligned training objective, and lightweight ensemble inference to better couple vocabulary quality with ranking performance. Experiments demonstrate consistent gains over strong baselines, indicating robust improvements in both accuracy and stability across diverse datasets.
